method: All packet inspection used installed tshark offline, with name resolution disabled (-n); no captured content was executed or sent onto a network.
The 18 destinations were selected from the existing published TH-0001 normal-P2P findings, then packet fields, TCP flags, payload lengths, and independent protocol dissections were inspected.
Rows with nested/comma-separated IPv4 addresses were excluded from TCP session counts so ICMP errors quoting an original TCP SYN were not counted as new TCP packets.
TCP flags are represented as True/False by this tshark version; sessions were grouped using its tcp.stream field. Payload sizes use tcp.len, not on-wire frame lengths.
The normal P2P capture has out-of-order timestamps. Listed start intervals follow packet order and include retransmissions where shown; they are wire diagnostics, not re-labelled detector output.

protocol_context.interpretation: Plaintext BitTorrent handshakes sent by the local host; the same peers also have opaque bidirectional payload sessions.
protocol_context.limitation: The opaque sessions cannot be passively identified as encrypted BitTorrent with certainty from these payloads; no blanket peer whitelist is justified.
protocol_context.dns_interpretation: The one resolver group aggregates different decoded query names. Favoring MAD over CV can make mixed traffic appear periodic.

limits: This is a profile of one publisher-verified normal P2P trace and two reviewed controlled positive captures, not field malware recall or general false-positive probability.
A stricter bidirectional payload requirement can discard one-way or partially observed sessions; it should not silently imply benignness.
The five mixed plaintext/opaque peer groups may remain noisy under the conservative first change; retain and report them honestly.
